name: Behentrimonium chloride

angle.text: Behentrimonium chloride is the waxy conditioning agent in many hair conditioners, used to make hair slippery, easier to detangle and less static so it looks smoother and sleeker. It is a background formulation ingredient rather than a standalone treatment, and it has not been tested on its own for appearance outcomes.

summary: Waxy cationic surfactant that makes conditioners slippery and anti-static; a formulation ingredient rather than a looksmaxxing treatment.
note: Can irritate at high concentration; toxic to aquatic life.
currentQuick:
Behentrimonium chloride is a positively charged fatty-chain compound found in many hair conditioners. It clings to the negatively charged surface of hair and is described as reducing static and tangling.
It is an ingredient, not a stand-alone treatment, and hair-specific clinical trials were not found.
How it works: Its charged head group is attracted to hair, while the long 22-carbon tail forms a lubricating layer on the strand.
Risks and caveats: Described as acceptable in rinse-off products at formulated levels but irritating to skin and eyes in concentrated form, and very toxic to aquatic life.
deepLead:
Behentrimonium chloride (also docosyltrimethylammonium chloride, BTAC-228) is a quaternary ammonium compound that acts as a cationic surfactant. It is a yellow, waxlike solid with the formula C25H54ClN.
It is used in cosmetics, chiefly hair conditioners, as an antistatic and conditioning agent; its positively charged head group binds to negatively charged hair surfaces, and its long fatty chain is described as smoothing the hair and reducing static.
Published research specific to its hair effects is limited, although studies of conditioner ingredients on hair and a post-marketing safety assessment of leave-on lotions containing it exist.

name: Polyquaternium-10

angle.text: Polyquaternium-10 is a cationic polymer in shampoos and conditioners that coats the hair, helping with combing, softness and manageability so hair looks smoother after washing. It appears as a background ingredient in hair-care products; there are no dedicated trials of it for appearance.

summary: Cationic cellulose polymer that coats hair in shampoos and conditioners; a background ingredient with no direct trials.
note: No hair-specific clinical or safety data found in the reviewed sources.
currentQuick:
Polyquaternium-10 is a modified cellulose with positive charges, used in shampoos and conditioners. Formulation literature credits cationic polymers with easier combing, smoother hair and better lather.
It is an ingredient rather than a treatment; no trials of it on hair were found.
How it works: Its positive charge attracts it to negatively charged hair, where it deposits as a thin conditioning film.
Risks and caveats: The reviewed sources report no specific safety findings for PQ-10 on hair or skin.
deepLead:
Polyquaternium-10 (PQ-10) is the INCI name for quaternized hydroxyethyl cellulose, a cellulose-derived polymer carrying positively charged quaternary ammonium groups. It belongs to the polyquaternium family, of which at least 40 members have been approved.
It is used in shampoos and conditioners, where cationic polymers are described as providing conditioning, smoothing, easier combing and creamier lather. It has also been studied in hydrogels, drug-delivery matrices and sensors.

name: Cetrimonium chloride

angle.text: Cetrimonium chloride is a common conditioner ingredient used to detangle and soften hair, giving a smoother, more manageable look after washing. Users of conditioners get this effect as part of the whole formula; the ingredient itself has not been studied for appearance outcomes, and contact-allergy reports are documented.

summary: Common conditioner surfactant that detangles and softens hair; a formulation ingredient with documented contact-allergy reports.
note: Reported as a possible contact irritant or allergen; concentrated form is corrosive.
currentQuick:
Cetrimonium chloride is a positively charged surfactant found in many conditioners, usually paired with fatty alcohols. It softens hair and reduces static.
It is an ingredient rather than a treatment, and no hair-appearance trials were found.
How it works: The positively charged head binds to negatively charged hair; with fatty alcohols and water it forms a creamy lamellar gel.
Risks and caveats: Dermatology reviews list it among quaternary ammonium compounds linked to contact dermatitis. Concentrated forms are corrosive and toxic to aquatic life, per Grokipedia.
deepLead:
Cetrimonium chloride (cetyltrimethylammonium chloride, CTAC) is a quaternary ammonium cationic surfactant, formula C19H42ClN, used in hair conditioners and shampoos and also as an antiseptic. In conditioners it is typically combined with long-chain fatty alcohols such as stearyl alcohol; the mixture forms a lamellar gel with water. Cationic surfactant levels are typically about 1 to 2 percent.
Grokipedia reports that the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel considered it safe in rinse-off products and at up to 0.25 percent in leave-on products when formulated to limit irritation. Dermatology literature lists it among quaternary ammonium compounds reported as contact allergens or irritants.

name: Keratin straightening

angle.text: Keratin straightening, or a Brazilian treatment, is a salon service used to reduce frizz and add shine, with results lasting roughly two to six months. The smoother look is visible right after the session; controlled trial data on the treatment are limited.

summary: Salon keratin-and-heat smoothing that lasts months; some products release formaldehyde, and trial data are scant.
note: Fumes and formaldehyde-releasing ingredients are a reported concern; not recommended in pregnancy.
currentQuick:
A keratin straightening treatment coats the hair with a keratin product and seals it with a flat iron, to cut frizz and add shine for a few months.
Published trial evidence is sparse: one small registered study with unknown status.
How it works: Heat sets the applied coating onto the hair shaft, smoothing the surface; it is described as less structurally permanent than relaxers.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes emitted gases, formaldehyde-releasing agents in some products, protective gear requirements, and advice against use in pregnancy. Heat can also damage hair.
deepLead:
Keratin straightening, also called a Brazilian treatment, is a salon smoothing procedure in which a keratin-containing product is applied to the hair and sealed in with a flat iron. Wikipedia describes it as reducing frizz and adding shine, lasting roughly two to six months, and taking about two to four hours.
The category has attracted health discussion. Wikipedia notes that keratin treatments emit gases, that skin and eye protection is required, and that they are not recommended during pregnancy; some straightening products are described as containing formaldehyde-releasing agents. Evidence for the treatments is limited: a small registered study of a keratin hair therapy exists, with unknown status.

name: Japanese thermal reconditioning

angle.text: Japanese thermal reconditioning (yuko or rebonding) is a salon process used to permanently straighten curly or wavy hair, giving a sleek, straight look that is visible immediately and stays in treated hair. No clinical trials were found; its use rests on salon practice and client experience.

summary: Salon chemical-plus-heat process that permanently straightens treated hair; no trials found, heat and scalp damage are reported risks.
note: Permanent for treated hair; reported heat damage, scalp irritation and hair loss.
currentQuick:
Japanese thermal reconditioning (yuko, rebonding) is a long salon process that uses a chemical to loosen hair bonds and heat to set the hair straight. The result is described as permanent for the treated length.
No clinical studies on it were found.
How it works: A chemical loosens cysteine bonds in the hair, then heat restructures them in a straight configuration.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include heat damage, scalp irritation and hair loss; new growth is not straightened.
deepLead:
Japanese thermal reconditioning, also called yuko or rebonding, is a salon procedure for permanently straightening hair. Wikipedia describes a non-coating chemical applied for about 15 to 20 minutes to loosen cysteine bonds, after which heat restructures the hair into a straight form; the full process takes about four to eight hours.
Because it chemically alters hair structure, new growth is unaffected and grows in with its natural texture. Reported concerns include heat damage, scalp irritation and hair loss, and damage from heat is described as irreversible short of cutting the hair off. No clinical studies were found specifically on it.

name: Sodium hydroxide relaxer

angle.text: A sodium hydroxide (lye) relaxer is the classic cream used to permanently straighten tight curls, giving a straight, smooth look in treated hair that is visible straight away; new growth comes in with its natural texture. Its straightening effect is well established in practice, while broader health associations are still under study.

summary: The classic lye cream that permanently straightens tight curls; strong on straightening, with documented scalp-burn risk and broader health associations under study.
note: Can cause chemical burns and breakage; relaxer use is associated with health outcomes in observational studies.
currentQuick:
A sodium hydroxide relaxer is the traditional 'lye' cream used to permanently straighten very curly hair. It is applied to the hair, not the roots of new growth, which keeps its natural texture.
It is a long-established cosmetic product, sold since the early twentieth century.
How it works: The strongly alkaline sodium hydroxide breaks the disulfide bonds in the hair shaft so curls can be straightened.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include scalp burns, dermatitis, dryness and breakage. Observational studies of relaxer use generally have linked it to fibroids and some cancers, though they do not distinguish lye from other types. Cosmetics are not pre-approved by the FDA.
deepLead:
A sodium hydroxide relaxer, commonly called a lye relaxer, is a cream-based chemical hair straightener that uses sodium hydroxide as its active alkali to permanently loosen tight curls. Lye creams typically combine sodium hydroxide, usually at about 5 to 10 percent, with petroleum jelly, mineral oil and emulsifiers, and have a pH of roughly 10 to 14. Relaxers act by breaking disulfide bonds in the hair shaft; the change applies only to treated hair and new growth emerges in its natural texture.
It is used mainly on coarse, tightly coiled hair and has a long history among African American women and men. Published research on relaxers has focused on health associations (fibroids, breast and uterine cancer) and on scalp and hair damage; these studies generally do not separate lye products from other relaxer types.

name: Calcium hydroxide relaxer

angle.text: Calcium hydroxide 'no-lye' relaxers are used to permanently straighten tight curls and are marketed as an option for sensitive scalps. The straightening is visible right after treatment; the claim of a gentler profile than lye relaxers has not been shown in studies.

summary: The 'no-lye' relaxer, billed as gentler on sensitive scalps than lye; no study has shown a different health profile.
note: Can still cause burns and breakage; health studies do not separate it from lye relaxers.
currentQuick:
A calcium hydroxide relaxer is the 'no-lye' alternative to the traditional sodium hydroxide cream, used to straighten tightly curled hair. It is mixed with a guanidine activator before use.
It is often marketed toward people with sensitive scalps.
How it works: Calcium hydroxide and guanidine carbonate react to form guanidine hydroxide, a weaker alkali that breaks the hair's disulfide bonds.
Risks and caveats: Burns, dermatitis and breakage are reported for both lye and no-lye relaxers. Observational health studies have not separated product types, and cosmetics are not pre-approved by the FDA.
deepLead:
A calcium hydroxide relaxer, marketed as a 'no-lye' relaxer, is a chemical hair straightener in which calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) is mixed at the time of use with an activating solution of guanidine carbonate, producing guanidine hydroxide as the active agent. Guanidine hydroxide is described as a weaker alkaline agent than sodium hydroxide, and these products are positioned as an option for sensitive scalps.
Like all relaxers, it permanently alters treated hair by breaking disulfide bonds, and new growth is unaffected. Wikipedia notes that both lye and no-lye relaxers can cause severe chemical burns and breakage, and that available health studies do not separate calcium-based products from sodium hydroxide ones.

name: Macassar oil

chain: Hair conditioned and held in place
angle.text: Macassar oil was a Victorian-era hair oil used by men to condition and style hair, giving a glossy, neat finish that is visible when applied. It was also advertised as promoting regrowth, a claim that rests on historical marketing rather than clinical trials.

summary: The Victorian hair oil that gave us the antimacassar; historically marketed for growth and styling, with no clinical evidence behind the growth claims.
note: Historical product; regrowth claims were advertising claims and have not been studied.
currentQuick:
Macassar oil was a perfumed vegetable-based hair oil popular with men in the 1800s. Alexander Rowland sold it from about 1793 and advertised it widely.
Its grease on chair backs gave rise to the antimacassar cloth.
How it works: It was a plain emollient hair dressing that coated and smoothed hair; advertised effects on growth have not been studied.
Risks and caveats: No specific harms are documented in the available sources. Its main historical drawback was staining of upholstery.
deepLead:
Macassar oil was a scented compound hair oil used mainly by men in Western Europe in the 19th and early 20th centuries to condition and style hair. It was popularised by the London barber Alexander Rowland, who from about 1793 sold Rowland's Macassar Oil, one of the first nationally advertised products. Advertisements made broad claims, including promoting hair regrowth.
Its name refers to the port of Makassar in Sulawesi, where ingredients were reputedly bought. The oil was greasy enough to stain furniture, which led to the antimacassar, a washable cloth protecting chair backs.

name: Jaw surgery / orthognathic

angle.text: Orthognathic surgery repositions the upper jaw, lower jaw and chin, and forum users treat it as the major structural option for a recessed jaw, facial balance and a straighter bite and smile. The change in jaw position is itself the visible result; reports note that functional gains and cosmetic outcomes do not always match.

currentQuick:
Orthognathic surgery is the medical term for jaw surgery that corrects the position of the upper jaw, lower jaw, chin or all three. It is used for underbites, overbites, open bites, asymmetry, jaw-joint problems and obstructive sleep apnoea, and it is also used to change facial proportions.
Looksmaxxing forums call it a hardmaxx procedure and discuss bimax, Le Fort I, genioplasty and related operations, with frequent questions about braces, insurance, recovery and complications. Medical literature documents functional outcomes and technique well, and is more limited on purely cosmetic goals.
How it works: Surgeons cut the jawbones from inside the mouth, move them to a planned position and fix them with titanium plates and screws, usually after orthodontic preparation. Virtual 3D planning, custom splints and patient-specific plates are increasingly used to transfer the plan to the operating room.
Risks and caveats: Reviews describe bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness, jaw-joint effects, relapse, hardware problems and a recovery of weeks to months. A systematic review also estimated that body dysmorphic disorder is more common among orthognathic surgery patients than in the general community.
deepLead:
Orthognathic surgery, also called corrective jaw surgery, reshapes the jaws and lower face to treat structural, growth, airway, jaw-joint and bite problems, and can also be used for facial balance and symmetry. The operation is usually done through the mouth: bone is cut, moved and fixed in a new position, and it is typically coordinated with orthodontic treatment.
Main procedures include the Le Fort I osteotomy for the upper jaw, the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy for the lower jaw, and genioplasty for the chin; surgeons may combine them in two-jaw (bimaxillary) surgery. Reviews describe expanding indications for upper-airway obstruction, computer-assisted planning, patient-specific fixation and shifts in the orthodontic-surgical sequence over the past two decades.
In looksmaxxing communities it is treated as one of the most consequential procedures, discussed alongside implants, rhinoplasty and orthodontics, with extensive talk about risk and surgeon choice.

name: Complementary eyeshadow for iris color
currentQuick:
This is a makeup tip: choose eyeshadow shades opposite your iris color on the color wheel so the eyes look more vivid.
It is based on color-theory reasoning, and no studies of its effect on perceived attractiveness were found.
How it works: Contrasting hues placed near the eye are said to increase the perceived saturation of the iris through simultaneous contrast.
Risks and caveats: No specific risks beyond general cosmetic precautions such as product allergies or irritation.
deepLead: Complementary eyeshadow for iris color is a makeup approach in which shadow colors are chosen to contrast with the eye's iris hue, on the color-wheel idea that opposite hues intensify each other. Practitioners say it makes the iris stand out.

name: Warm / cool light & colored backgrounds for photos
currentQuick:
Some people choose warm or cool light and colored backgrounds to make eye color look more vivid in photographs.
The idea comes from color-matching advice, and no studies were found.
How it works: Background and light color are said to change how saturated the iris appears relative to its surroundings.
Risks and caveats: No risks beyond the limited reliability of an unstudied technique.
deepLead: Warm or cool lighting and colored backgrounds are photography choices that some appearance communities say can make eye color look stronger in photos by color contrast.

name: FaceTune / AI eye whitening
currentQuick:
Photo apps such as FaceTune offer tools to whiten the eyes and brighten the iris in pictures.
These edits change the photograph only, and no research on them was found.
How it works: Software selects the eye region and increases brightness or saturation, sometimes using AI segmentation.
Risks and caveats: No physical risks; critics of heavy retouching in general raise concerns about unrealistic image standards, though no study specific to eye whitening was found.
deepLead: FaceTune and similar photo-editing apps include tools that brighten or whiten the sclera and iris in photographs. Some appearance communities discuss using such edits to make eyes look brighter.

name: Reading aloud practice
currentQuick:
Reading aloud practice means regularly voicing written text with attention to pacing, enunciation and expression. In voice-improvement discussions it is described as a way to work on cadence and clarity.
No studies or reference articles were found examining it as a looksmaxxing practice, so its effects on perceived attractiveness are untested.
How it works: Practitioners describe repeated oral reading as a way to rehearse articulation and pacing in a controlled setting, often combined with recording and playback.
Risks and caveats: No risks are documented. Prolonged loud speaking can strain the voice, which is general voice-care guidance rather than a finding specific to this practice.
deepLead:
Reading aloud practice is the habit of voicing written text on purpose, with attention to cadence, articulation and clarity. It appears in voice-improvement discussions as a low-cost exercise, often paired with recording oneself.
No published studies or encyclopedia sources were identified that evaluate it as a method of changing how a voice is perceived, so this entry is brief.

name: Recording yourself
currentQuick:
Recording yourself means capturing your speech on a phone or microphone and listening back to get feedback on how you sound. In voice-improvement discussions it is treated as a basic feedback step.
No studies were found testing it for changing perceived attractiveness or authority.
How it works: Playback lets a speaker hear pacing, filler words and tone from outside, which practitioners say differs from how one hears oneself while talking.
Risks and caveats: No risks are documented in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Recording yourself is the practice of capturing one's speech or voice and listening back to review it. In voice-improvement communities it is described as a feedback tool used alongside exercises such as reading aloud or slowing one's pace.
No studies were found that test self-recording as a voice or appearance intervention, so this entry is brief.

name: Slowing speech and pausing
currentQuick:
This practice involves deliberately lowering speech rate and inserting pauses, which advocates say conveys composure and authority.
No reference sources or studies on it were located for this entry, so its claimed effect is untested here.
How it works: Proponents say slower delivery and deliberate silences make speech seem more controlled and give listeners time to absorb points.
Risks and caveats: No risks are documented in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Slowing speech and pausing refers to deliberately reducing speaking rate and using silences to shape delivery. In voice-improvement discussions it is described as a way to project authority.
No published studies or reference articles were identified for this entry, so no evidence on its effect on perception can be summarized.

name: Low-glycemic diet (for acne)

angle.text: People with acne adopt a low-glycemic diet hoping that steadier blood sugar will reduce breakouts and give clearer skin. It is among the few diet changes with some trial support for acne, though the evidence is modest.

currentQuick:
A low-glycemic diet swaps fast-digesting carbohydrates such as white bread, sugary drinks and sweets for slower ones such as legumes, whole grains and most vegetables. In looksmaxxing and skincare circles it is discussed as a way to reduce acne without drugs.
According to Wikipedia's acne article, several randomized and non-randomized studies have reported that lower-glycemic-load diets reduced acne severity, and dermatologists commonly suggest a diet low in simple sugars. The overall body of evidence is described as emerging rather than settled.
How it works: The proposed mechanism is that high-glycemic meals raise blood glucose and insulin, which is thought to increase IGF-1 and androgen activity, and in turn sebum production and comedone formation. Androgens and IGF-1 are both considered important in acne biology.
Risks and caveats: A low-GI eating pattern is generally an ordinary dietary approach with no specific safety concerns identified in the sources. Glycemic index is an imperfect measure: some foods with a low GI are high in fat or sugar, and values vary between individuals and preparations.
deepLead:
A low-glycemic diet (low-GI or low-glycemic-load diet) is an eating pattern built around foods that raise blood glucose slowly, used by some people with acne in the hope of reducing breakouts. The glycemic index, introduced by David Jenkins and colleagues in 1981, ranks carbohydrate foods from 0 to 100 against pure glucose, and glycemic load adjusts that ranking for portion size.
Wikipedia's acne article reports that multiple randomized controlled trials and non-randomized studies found a lower-glycemic-load diet effective in reducing acne, and that dermatologists recommend a diet low in simple sugars. The same article describes the evidence for diet and acne as emerging, and says a causal relationship between diet and skin conditions is rarely observed.
Glycemic index itself has recognized limitations: values depend on ripeness, cooking and processing, individual responses differ, and some foods with a low GI are otherwise energy-dense.
